fields.title: The Gospel of Mark
fields.subtitle: Kata Markon, “According to Mark”
fields.description: The shortest of the four Gospels, and probably the first to be written: “The beginning of the gospel about Jesus Christ.” Fast and vivid, it moves from the Jordan to Galilee at once, where Jesus heals, casts out unclean spirits, stills the storm and leaves his disciples asking, “Who is this?” Then the way to Jerusalem, three times foretelling his death, and the saying at the heart of the book, that the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as the ransom price for many. The cross, where a Roman centurion is the first to call him God’s Son, and an empty tomb, where frightened women hear that he has gone ahead of them to Galilee. Traditionally the memories of Peter, written down by his interpreter Mark. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Gospel of Mark?
qa.answer: The second and shortest of the four Gospels, the accounts of the life, death and resurrection of Jesus in the New Testament. It tells the story quickly and vividly, from John the Baptist at the Jordan to the empty tomb, with about a third of the book given to the last week of Jesus’s life. Its centre is the question of who Jesus is, and its answer is that he is the Son of God who came “to give his life as the ransom price for many” (10:45).

qa.question: Who wrote the Gospel of Mark, and when?
qa.answer: The Gospel does not name its author. From the earliest tradition it has been called Mark’s, identified with John Mark of Acts, a companion of Paul and Barnabas and later of Peter. Papias, early in the second century, said that Mark was Peter’s interpreter and wrote down accurately what Peter remembered of what Jesus said and did. Most scholars date it to the late 60s or around AD 70, and tradition places it in Rome.

qa.question: Was Mark the first Gospel to be written?
qa.answer: Most scholars think so. Nearly all of Mark is found in Matthew and Luke, often in the same order and wording, and the usual explanation is that both of them used Mark. Others hold, as Augustine did, that Matthew came first and Mark abridged it. The question does not change what any of the Gospels says, but it helps explain why the first three are so alike.

qa.question: What is the “messianic secret” in Mark?
qa.answer: A name scholars give to the way Jesus in Mark tells demons to be silent, tells people he has healed to tell no one, and orders his disciples not to say he is the Christ (8:30). Part of the reason may be that crowds would have taken him for the wrong kind of Messiah. Mark’s deeper point is that no one can understand who Jesus is until they have seen the cross, where a centurion at last says, “This man really was God’s Son!” (15:39).

qa.question: How does the Gospel of Mark end?
qa.answer: In the two oldest complete manuscripts it ends at 16:8, with women running from the empty tomb, telling no one, “for they were afraid”. Whether Mark meant to end there or his ending was lost is an open question. Most later manuscripts add a longer ending (16:9–20), and a few have a short ending; neither is in Mark’s style. Like most Bibles, this edition prints both after 16:8, set apart and in brackets, with a note.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
The beginning of the gospel about Jesus Christ.

— Mark 1:1

Mark has no time for a nativity. There are no shepherds, no wise men, no family tree. His first sentence is a title, and by the fourteenth verse Jesus is already grown, baptized, tested in the wilderness and walking into Galilee with a message: the time has come, the kingdom of God has come near. From then on the story hardly pauses for breath.

It is the shortest of the four Gospels, and for a long time it was the least read. Nearly everything in it is also in Matthew or Luke, usually at greater length, and early readers tended to prefer the fuller versions. The modern world has rediscovered it. Mark is vivid, blunt and fast. It shows Jesus angry and grieved and deeply moved; it shows his disciples baffled, frightened and slow; and it ends, in its oldest form, in a way no one expects. It reads less like a book about Jesus than like an eyewitness telling you what it was like to be there.

And the first word of its title is the right one. This is “the beginning of the gospel”, the good news. It may be from Mark’s use of the word that the four books came to be called Gospels.

Peter’s memories

The Gospel does not name its author. From the earliest days it has been called Mark’s, and the church has identified him with John Mark of the book of Acts, whose mother’s house in Jerusalem was a meeting place for the first believers. He set out with Paul and his cousin Barnabas on their first journey, turned back halfway, and became the cause of a quarrel so sharp that the two missionaries parted company. Years later Paul writes of him as a fellow worker and asks for him by name, “because he is helpful to me in my work”. The first letter of Peter sends greetings from Rome, under the name Babylon, from “my son Mark”.

It is Peter that the early tradition links him with most closely. Papias, a bishop in Asia Minor early in the second century, passed on what he had been told by an older teacher:

“Mark, having become the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately, though not in order, whatsoever he remembered of the things said or done by Christ.”

Irenaeus, around 180, says the same: Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, handed down in writing what Peter had preached. Many readers have felt Peter’s voice behind the book. Peter is the first disciple called and the last named; the story often seems told from where he stood; and his failures are told without softening. The details are those of someone who remembered: the cushion in the stern of the boat where Jesus slept in the storm, the green grass where the five thousand sat down, the young man in a linen sheet who ran away naked on the night of the arrest.

Most scholars date the book to the late 60s or around AD 70, and the tradition places it in Rome, among Christians who had recently suffered under Nero. Mark explains Jewish customs and translates Aramaic words, so his first readers were not, for the most part, Jews of Judea. Most scholars also think it was the first of the Gospels to be written, and that Matthew and Luke both used it, though some hold, as Augustine did, that Matthew came first. On either view it is the Gospel closest to the way the apostles first told the story aloud.

At once

Mark’s favourite word is a small Greek word meaning “immediately”, and he uses it more than forty times. Jesus comes up out of the water and at once sees the heavens torn open; the Spirit at once drives him out into the wilderness; the fishermen at once leave their nets; he goes at once into the synagogue. The effect is of a story told breathlessly, by someone who cannot wait to get to what happened next.

Mark also loves to tell stories in the present tense, and to sandwich one story inside another. Jairus begs Jesus to come and heal his dying daughter; on the way a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years touches his cloak; by the time Jesus has found her, word comes that the girl is dead. Jesus curses a fig tree, then drives the traders out of the temple, and the next morning the fig tree is found withered. Peter follows Jesus into the high priest’s courtyard; inside, Jesus is tried and confesses who he is; outside, Peter denies three times that he knows him. Each story helps us read the other.

Who is this?

The first half of Mark is driven by a single question. Jesus teaches with an authority the scribes do not have. He orders unclean spirits out, and they go. He forgives a paralysed man’s sins and then, to show that he has the right to, tells him to get up and walk. He touches a leper, eats with tax collectors, and calls himself the Lord of the Sabbath. And one night on the lake he wakes in the stern of a sinking boat and speaks to the wind:

Jesus woke, rebuked the wind, and commanded the sea, “Silence! Be still!” The wind dropped, and a great calm came over the water.

— Mark 4:39

The disciples are more frightened afterwards than they were in the storm. “Who is this, then,” they ask one another, “that wind and sea alike obey him?” Every reader of the Old Testament knew who commands the sea. The disciples do not yet dare to say it.

Strangely, those who see most clearly in these chapters are the demons, who shout out that he is God’s Holy One and the Son of the Most High God, and Jesus silences them. He tells the people he heals to tell no one, and later he orders his disciples not to say who he is. Scholars have called this the “messianic secret”. Part of the reason may be practical: a crowd that wanted a miracle-worker or a warrior king could easily take him for the wrong kind of Messiah. But Mark’s deeper point is that no one can understand who Jesus is until they have seen the cross.

And yet no Gospel shows Jesus more plainly as a man. In Mark the people of Nazareth know him as “the carpenter, the son of Mary”, and take offence. His own family set out to take charge of him, saying, “He has lost his senses.” He sleeps from exhaustion, groans, is angry with his own disciples, and looks at a rich man and loves him. Of the day and hour of the end he says that nobody knows it, “neither the angels in heaven nor the Son.” Mark does not set the man and the mystery against each other. The one who commands the sea is the one asleep on the cushion.

On the way

The middle of the book is framed by two healings of blind men. At Bethsaida a man is healed in two stages: at first he sees people “like trees moving about”, and only with a second touch can he see everything clearly. That is exactly where the disciples are. At Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks who they say he is, and Peter answers for them all:

Peter answered, “You are the Christ.”

— Mark 8:29

He is right, and he cannot yet see what it means. As soon as Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected and be killed, and rise again after three days, Peter takes him aside and rebukes him, and Jesus rebukes him back: “Get behind me, Satan!”

Three times in these chapters Jesus foretells his death, and three times the disciples miss the point. After the first, Peter protests. After the second, they argue on the road about which of them is the greatest. After the third, James and John ask for the best seats in his glory. And each time Jesus teaches them what it means to follow him: to say no to themselves and take up their cross, to be last of all and servant of all. The section reaches its summit in a single sentence, perhaps the key to the whole Gospel:

The Son of Man himself came, not so that others would serve him, but to serve them and to give his life as the ransom price for many.”

— Mark 10:45

Then, at Jericho, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus shouts for mercy, throws off his cloak, receives his sight, and follows Jesus “along the road”. The word for road is the same word Mark has used for “the way” all through these chapters. The man who sees follows Jesus on the way to Jerusalem, and to the cross.

The disciples

No Gospel is harder on the Twelve than Mark. They are called, sent out with power, and given the mystery of the kingdom. And they are, again and again, without understanding. They panic in the storm. They forget the loaves the day after the feeding. Jesus asks them, “Do you still not see it or understand? Have your hearts been hardened?”, words Mark used earlier of Jesus’s opponents. In Gethsemane they sleep. At the arrest “they all left him and ran.” Peter, who promised to die with him, swears he does not know him.

Others in Mark see more clearly: a leper, a desperate father who cries, “I believe! Help my unbelief!”, a woman who pours a flask of costly perfume over Jesus’s head and is told that wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her. And when the men have fled, it is the women who stay, watching from a distance at the cross and coming to the tomb.

Mark tells this not to shame the apostles, who were the church’s leaders by the time he wrote, but to give hope to every disciple who has failed. If Jesus could make apostles of these men, there is hope for anyone. The first message from the empty tomb includes a name: “go and tell his disciples, and Peter too”.

The cross

About a third of Mark is taken up with the last week of Jesus’s life, and his account of the cross is the starkest of the four. There are no words of comfort from the cross. Jesus is mocked by the passers-by, the chief priests and the men crucified with him. Darkness falls at noon. At three in the afternoon he cries out in Aramaic, in the words of Psalm 22, and then dies with a loud cry.

Mark draws two lines from the beginning of his book to this moment. At the baptism the heavens were “torn apart” and a voice said, “You are my dearly loved Son.” Now the curtain of the temple is split in two, the same Greek word, and a voice is heard again, this time from the most unlikely person in the story:

The centurion standing in front of him saw how he died, and he said, “This man really was God’s Son!”

— Mark 15:39

The first human being in Mark to call Jesus the Son of God is a Gentile, a Roman officer, and he says it not after a miracle but after watching him die. That is what the whole book has been leading to. Jesus is most clearly the Son of God not when he stills the storm but when he gives his life as a ransom for many.

The ending

On the first day of the week, three women come to the tomb with spices and find the stone rolled away. A young man in white tells them that Jesus has been raised and is going ahead of them to Galilee. And in the oldest manuscripts, that is where the Gospel ends:

They went out and ran from the tomb, trembling and beside themselves. And they told no one anything, for they were afraid.

— Mark 16:8

It is a startling last line, and in Greek it ends on the word “for”. Whether Mark meant to stop here, or his ending was lost, no one knows. Early copyists clearly felt that something more was needed, and two later endings were written to round it off. But many readers have come to think Mark meant exactly this. The promise has been given; the reader knows the message was in the end delivered, or there would be no Gospel to read. And the book leaves us standing at the empty tomb, with the women, asking what we will do with the news.

How to read Mark

Mark is short enough to read aloud in a little over an hour, and that is the best way to meet it first, as its first hearers did. Notice its shape: the beginning by the Jordan (1:1–13); the work in Galilee, with its question “Who is this?” (1:14–8:26); the way to Jerusalem, with its answer and its teaching on the cross (8:27–10:52); and the last week in Jerusalem, from the entry into the city to the empty tomb (11–16).

Then read it slowly. Watch Jesus’s face: Mark tells us when he looks around, when he groans, when he is angry, when he looks at a rich young man and loves him. Watch the disciples, and ask where you would have been standing. And watch for the moments when Mark speaks over the heads of the characters to the reader, as in the middle of Jesus’s words about the end: “What I tell you, I tell everyone: Keep watch!”

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Mark are worth knowing about before you begin.

“Immediately.” Rather than repeat one English word forty times, the translation varies it (“the moment”, “straight away”, “at once”, “on the spot”), so that Mark’s pace is felt without becoming monotonous.

The first verse. Many manuscripts add “the Son of God” to the title in 1:1; a few early ones lack it. This translation follows the shorter text, “The beginning of the gospel about Jesus Christ.” Mark gives Jesus that title at the key moments all the same, from the voice at the baptism to the centurion at the cross.

Jesus’s anger. In 1:41, where most manuscripts say Jesus was moved with pity for a leper, this translation follows one early Greek manuscript (Codex Bezae) and some Old Latin copies that say he was “Stirred with anger”, the harder reading, which copyists were more likely to soften than to invent. Mark speaks of Jesus’s anger elsewhere too.

The endings. The two later endings are printed after 16:8, set apart and in brackets, with a note: a short ending, in which the women report to Peter and his companions, and the longer ending (16:9–20), found in most manuscripts but not in the earliest, which tells of appearances to Mary Magdalene, to two disciples and to the eleven. Their style and vocabulary are not Mark’s, and they read like a summary of appearances told in the other Gospels and Acts. They are part of the church’s Bible and are printed here, as in most Bibles, with that note.

Verses not in the oldest manuscripts. Mark 7:16, 9:44, 9:46, 11:26 and 15:28, which older Bibles print, are missing from the earliest copies and were probably repeated from other verses or other Gospels. They are not in the text, and the verse numbers are skipped.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Mark 1
fields.body_html:
1The beginning of the gospel about Jesus Christ.

The messenger in the wilderness

2It happened just as it is written in the prophet Isaiah: “See, I am sending my messenger ahead of you; he will make your road ready. 3A voice is calling out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, straighten the roads he will travel.’” 4Then John the Baptizer came on the scene in the wilderness, calling people to a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of their sins. 5The whole land of Judea and everyone from Jerusalem kept going out to him. They confessed their sins, and he baptized them in the Jordan River. 6John’s clothes were made of camel’s hair, and he had a leather belt around his waist. He lived on locusts and wild honey. 7This was his message: “Someone stronger than I am is coming after me. I am not fit even to bend down and untie the strap of his sandals. 8The baptism I gave you was with water; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

Jesus is baptized

9It was during those days that Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee, and John baptized him in the Jordan. 10The moment he came up out of the water, he saw the heavens torn apart and the Spirit coming down on him like a dove. 11Then a voice spoke from heaven: “You are my dearly loved Son. I take delight in you.”

Forty days in the wilderness

12Straight away the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness. 13He stayed in the wilderness for forty days while Satan tempted him. He was among the wild animals, and the angels took care of him.

The kingdom of God has come near

14After John had been handed over, Jesus went into Galilee, proclaiming God’s gospel. 15“The appointed time has arrived in full,” he said, “and the kingdom of God has come near. Repent, and believe in the gospel.”

Four fishermen follow Jesus

16As Jesus went along the shore of the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Simon’s brother Andrew throwing a net into the water. They fished for a living. 17Jesus said to them, “Come and follow me. I will make you into fishers of people.” 18They dropped their nets on the spot and followed him. 19He went on a little way and saw James son of Zebedee and his brother John, who were in their boat putting their nets in order. 20He called them at once. Leaving their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired workers, they went off after him.

A new teaching, with authority

21They made their way to Capernaum. On the Sabbath he went straight into the synagogue and taught there. 22His teaching astounded them. Unlike the scribes, he taught them as someone who has authority. 23Right then, in their synagogue, there was a man with an unclean spirit, and he screamed, 24“What do you have to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Are you here to destroy us? I know who you are: God’s Holy One!” 25Jesus ordered it sternly, “Silence! Come out of the man!” 26The unclean spirit threw the man into a fit, gave a loud shriek, and left him. 27Amazement seized them all, and they talked it over among themselves: “What is this? A new kind of teaching, backed by authority! At his command even the unclean spirits do as they are told.” 28The news about him went out at once in every direction, through all the country around Galilee.

Simon’s mother-in-law

29They left the synagogue and went straight to the house where Simon and Andrew lived, and James and John came with them. 30Simon’s mother-in-law lay ill with a fever, and they lost no time in telling him about her. 31He came over, took hold of her hand, and lifted her up. Her fever was gone, and she started to look after them.

The whole town at the door

32When evening came and the sun had set, people began bringing to him everyone who was ill or controlled by demons. 33The entire town had crowded together outside the door. 34He cured many people who had diseases of every kind, and he threw out many demons. He did not permit the demons to say anything, since they knew him.

On to the nearby towns

35Long before daylight, he got up and went out. He went off to a lonely place and spent time there in prayer. 36Simon and the others with him tracked him down. 37Finding him, they said, “Everybody is out looking for you!” 38He replied, “Let us move on to the market towns nearby, so that I can proclaim the message there as well. This is what I came out to do.” 39He went into their synagogues all over Galilee, where he proclaimed the message and threw out demons.

A man with a skin disease is made clean

40A man with a serious skin disease came to him. Falling on his knees, he pleaded with him, “If you are willing, you have the power to make me clean.” 41Stirred with anger, he stretched out his hand and touched him. “I am willing,” he told him. “Be made clean!” 42In that moment the disease was gone from him, and he was clean. 43Jesus gave him a stern warning and sent him away at once. 44“Be sure you tell no one about this,” he said. “Instead, go and let the priest examine you. Then offer what Moses required for your cleansing. That will be evidence to them.” 45But the man went off and began telling everyone, spreading the news of what had happened, so much that Jesus could not go into any town openly anymore. He kept to deserted places out in the country, and still people came to him from every direction.
fields.summary: John the Baptizer prepares the way in the wilderness, and Jesus is baptized, tested for forty days, and begins to proclaim that the kingdom of God has come near. Jesus calls four fishermen, teaches with authority in Capernaum, drives out unclean spirits and heals many, among them Simon’s mother-in-law and a man with a serious skin disease.

fields.title: Mark 2
fields.body_html:
Let down through the roof

1Some days later he came back to Capernaum, and word got around that he was at home. 2So many people crowded in that there was no space left, even outside the door, and he spoke the word to them. 3Then some people arrived with a paralyzed man for him, carried by four of them. 4The crowd kept them from getting him near Jesus, so they took off part of the roof above where he was. They broke through it and lowered the mat with the paralyzed man lying on it. 5Jesus saw how they trusted in him, and he said to the paralyzed man, “My child, your sins are forgiven.” 6Some of the scribes were sitting there, and they were asking themselves, 7“Why does this fellow talk this way? It is blasphemy! Who but God alone can forgive sins?” 8At once Jesus knew in his spirit what they were thinking. “Why do you turn these things over in your hearts?” he asked them. 9“What is easier to say to this paralyzed man: ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or ‘Get up, take your mat, and walk’? 10But I want you to be sure of this: the Son of Man has the right on earth to forgive sins.” Then he turned to the paralyzed man. 11“Get up, I tell you. Take your mat and go home.” 12He got up, picked up his mat at once, and walked out while they all watched. They were all astonished and gave glory to God. “We have never seen anything like it!” they said.

Levi leaves his tax office

13Once more he went out along the lakeshore. The whole crowd kept coming to him, and he taught them. 14As he walked along, he caught sight of Levi son of Alphaeus sitting in the tax office. “Follow me,” he said to him. He got up and followed him.

A meal with tax collectors and sinners

15Later Jesus was having a meal in Levi’s house, and many tax collectors and sinners shared the table with him and his disciples. There were many such people among those who followed him. 16Some scribes who were Pharisees saw him eating with sinners and tax collectors, and they asked his disciples, “Why is he eating with tax collectors and sinners?” 17Jesus heard it and told them, “People who are well do not need a doctor; sick people do. I came to call sinners, not the righteous.”

While the bridegroom is with them

18John’s disciples and the Pharisees were keeping a fast. People came and asked him, “John’s disciples fast, and so do the Pharisees’ disciples. Why do your disciples not fast?” 19Jesus answered, “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is there with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, fasting is out of the question. 20But days are coming when the bridegroom will be taken from them; on that day they will fast.

21Nobody sews a piece of new, unshrunk cloth onto an old coat. If they did, the new patch would shrink and tear away from the old cloth, and the hole would get worse. 22And nobody pours new wine into old wineskins. If they did, the wine would split the skins, and both wine and skins would be lost. New wine needs new skins.”

The Sabbath was made for people

23One Sabbath Jesus was going through the grainfields, and as his disciples made their way along, they started to pick heads of grain. 24The Pharisees said to him, “See there! Why are they doing something on the Sabbath that the law forbids?” 25He answered, “Have you not read what David did when he and his men were in need and hungry? 26In the days of Abiathar the high priest, he went into the house of God and ate the bread set out before God, which the law allows only the priests to eat. He even gave some to the men with him.” 27Then he said to them, “The Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath. 28So the Son of Man is Lord even over the Sabbath.”
fields.summary: Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man let down through a roof, calls Levi from his tax office and eats with tax collectors and sinners. Questioned about fasting and the Sabbath, Jesus answers that the Sabbath was made for people and that the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.

fields.title: Mark 3
fields.body_html:
A withered hand on the Sabbath

1Once again he went into the synagogue. A man was there whose hand was withered. 2They kept a close eye on Jesus to see if he would heal the man on the Sabbath, so that they could bring a charge against him. 3Jesus told the man whose hand was withered, “Get up and come out here in front.” 4Then he asked them, “What does the law allow on the Sabbath: doing good or doing harm, saving a life or killing?” They said nothing. 5He looked around at them in anger, deeply grieved that their hearts were so hard, and said to the man, “Hold out your hand.” He held it out, and it was made well again. 6The Pharisees left, and at once they began making plans with the Herodians about how to destroy him.

Crowds from every region

7Jesus went off with his disciples to the lake, and a large crowd from Galilee followed. 8Hearing about all that he was doing, a great many people also came to him from Judea and Jerusalem, from Idumea and the land beyond the Jordan, and from the area around Tyre and Sidon. 9Because of the crowd, he told his disciples to keep a small boat ready for him, so that he would not be crushed. 10He had healed many, and so all who had diseases kept pushing forward to touch him. 11Whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they threw themselves down in front of him and shouted, “You are the Son of God!” 12But he sternly ordered them not to make him known.

Twelve chosen to be with him

13Then he went up into the hills and called to him the ones he wanted, and they came to him. 14He appointed twelve to be with him, and to be sent out to proclaim the message 15with authority to throw out demons. 16So he appointed the twelve. To Simon he gave the name Peter. 17James son of Zebedee and John, James’s brother, he called Boanerges, that is, “Sons of Thunder.” 18Then there were Andrew and Philip, Bartholomew and Matthew, Thomas and James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus and Simon the Cananaean, 19and Judas Iscariot, who went on to betray him.

The strong man is bound

20Then he went home, and again such a crowd gathered that they could not even eat a meal. 21When his family heard about this, they set out to take charge of him, because they were saying, “He has lost his senses.” 22Scribes who had come down from Jerusalem claimed, “Beelzebul has hold of him!” and, “It is by the ruler of the demons that he throws out demons!” 23So he called them over and spoke to them in parables: “How can Satan throw out Satan? 24If a kingdom splits into sides that fight each other, it cannot last. 25If a household turns against itself, it will not hold together. 26So if Satan has rebelled against himself and is divided, he cannot last; his end has come. 27In fact, no one can break into a strong man’s house and carry off his belongings without first tying him up. Only then can he rob the house.

28Truly I tell you, people will be forgiven all their sins and all the blasphemies they speak, however many they may be. 29But anyone who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness, ever; that person is guilty of an eternal sin.” 30Jesus spoke this way because they were claiming, “He has an unclean spirit.”

Whoever does the will of God

31Then his mother and brothers arrived. They stood outside and sent word in, asking for him. 32A crowd was sitting around him, and they told him, “Look, your mother and brothers are outside, and they want you.” 33He answered, “Who is my mother? Who are my brothers?” 34He looked at the people sitting in a circle around him and said, “See, these are my mother and my brothers! 35Whoever does what God wants is my brother and sister and mother.”
fields.summary: Jesus heals a withered hand on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees begin to plot with the Herodians. Crowds come from every region; Jesus chooses the Twelve, answers the charge of driving out demons by Beelzebul, and says that whoever does the will of God is brother, sister and mother.

fields.title: Mark 4
fields.body_html:
A farmer goes out to sow

1Once more he began teaching by the lake. The crowd that gathered around him was so enormous that he stepped into a boat and sat in it out on the water, while all the people stayed on the shore by the lake. 2He used parables to teach them many things, and as he taught he said to them, 3“Listen! A farmer went out to sow seed. 4As he scattered it, some seed fell beside the path, and birds came and ate it up. 5Some fell on rocky ground, where there was little soil. It came up quickly, since the soil was shallow. 6But when the sun came up, the young plants were scorched, and having no root they dried up. 7Other seed fell among thorny weeds, which grew up and choked it, so that it produced no grain. 8But other seed fell on good soil. It came up, grew, and produced a crop, yielding thirty, sixty, even a hundred times what was sown.” 9Then he said, “Anyone who has ears to hear should listen.”

Why Jesus speaks in parables

10When he was by himself, the Twelve and the others around him asked him about the parables. 11He told them, “You have been given the mystery of the kingdom of God. But for those outside, everything comes in parables, 12so that they may look and look but never perceive, and listen and listen but never understand; otherwise they might turn back and be forgiven.”

The seed is the word

13Then he said to them, “Do you not see what this parable means? How then will you understand all the others? 14The farmer sows the word. 15Some are like seed sown beside the path. When the word is sown in them and they hear it, Satan comes at once and carries off the word that was planted in them. 16In the same way, others are like seed sown on rocky ground. When they hear the word, they welcome it at once with joy, 17but it takes no root in them, and they last only a short while. Then, when hardship or persecution arises on account of the word, they soon fall away. 18Still others are like seed sown among thorns. They hear the word, 19but worries about this present age, the false promise of wealth, and longing for other things crowd in and smother the word, so that it bears no fruit. 20But others are like seed sown in good soil. These hear the word, welcome it, and bear a crop, thirty, sixty, or a hundred times what was sown.”

Nothing hidden that will not come to light

21He also said to them, “Is a lamp brought in to be set under a bowl or under a bed? Is it not meant to go on a lampstand? 22For nothing is hidden except to be brought out in the open, and nothing has been kept secret except so that it might come to light. 23If anyone has ears to hear, let that person listen.” 24He also said to them, “Pay attention to what you hear. Whatever measure you use, God will use the same for you, and will give you more besides. 25Those who have will be given more, and those who do not have will lose even what they have.”

Seed that grows by itself

26He also said, “It is like this with the kingdom of God: a man throws seed on the ground. 27He goes to sleep at night and gets up by day, and the seed sprouts and grows tall, though he does not know how. 28The earth bears its crop on its own: first the green blade, then the ear, then the ear full of grain. 29And when the grain is ready, he puts in the sickle at once, because harvest time has come.”

The smallest of seeds

30He also said, “What shall we liken the kingdom of God to? What parable shall we set beside it? 31It is like a mustard seed. When it is sown in the ground, it is smaller than every other seed on earth. 32But once it is sown, it shoots up and becomes bigger than all the garden plants. It sends out branches so large that the birds of the sky can settle in its shade.”

33With many parables like these he spoke the word to them, as much as they were able to hear. 34He would say nothing to them without a parable, but in private he made everything plain to his own disciples.

Even the wind and the sea obey him

35As evening came on that day, Jesus said to his disciples, “Let us go across to the far side of the lake.” 36They sent the crowd away and took him along in the boat, since he was already in it. Other boats also went with him. 37A fierce windstorm blew up, and the waves were crashing into the boat, so that it was already filling with water. 38Jesus himself was asleep on the cushion at the back of the boat. They woke him and said, “Teacher, does it mean nothing to you that we are going to die?” 39Jesus woke, rebuked the wind, and commanded the sea, “Silence! Be still!” The wind dropped, and a great calm came over the water. 40Then he asked them, “Why are you so afraid? Is there still no faith in you?” 41Great fear came over them, and they kept saying to one another, “Who is this, then, that wind and sea alike obey him?”
fields.summary: From a boat Jesus teaches in parables: the sower, the lamp, the seed that grows by itself and the mustard seed. That evening on the lake Jesus calms a great storm, and the disciples ask who this is, that even the wind and the sea obey.

fields.title: Mark 5
fields.body_html:
A man called Legion

1They reached the far side of the lake, the country of the Gerasenes. 2As soon as he stepped out of the boat, a man with an unclean spirit came out from the tombs to meet him. 3This man lived among the tombs, and nobody could keep him tied up anymore, not even with a chain. 4Time and again he had been bound hand and foot with irons and chains, but he had pulled the chains apart and smashed the irons on his feet. No one had the strength to control him. 5Night and day, without stopping, he would scream among the tombs and on the hills and slash himself with stones. 6When he caught sight of Jesus a long way off, he ran up and threw himself down in front of him. 7He gave a loud shriek: “Jesus, Son of the Most High God, what have you to do with me? I beg you, with God as witness, do not torture me!” 8This was because Jesus had been telling it, “Unclean spirit, come out of this man!” 9Then Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He answered, “My name is Legion, since there are many of us.” 10He kept pleading with Jesus not to send them away out of that country. 11A large herd of pigs happened to be grazing on the hillside nearby. 12The spirits pleaded with him, “Send us over to the pigs. Let us go into them.” 13He gave them leave. Out came the unclean spirits, and they went into the pigs. The whole herd, about 2,000 animals, stampeded down the steep slope into the lake and drowned there.

14The men tending the pigs ran off and spread the news in the town and on the farms, and people came out to see what had taken place. 15When they reached Jesus, they found the man the demons had held sitting there with clothes on and in his right mind, the very man who had been held by the legion. And they were afraid. 16Those who had seen it all told them what had happened to the man with the demons, and about the pigs too. 17Then they started pleading with Jesus to go away from their district. 18As Jesus stepped into the boat, the man freed from the demons pleaded to go along with him. 19But Jesus would not let him, and told him instead, “Go home to your own people, and let them know all that the Lord has done for you, and the mercy he has shown you.” 20So he went off and started to tell all through the Decapolis the great things Jesus had done for him. Everyone who heard was astonished.

Jairus pleads for his daughter

21When Jesus had gone back across by boat, a large crowd gathered around him while he was still by the lake. 22One of the leaders of the synagogue, a man named Jairus, came up. When he saw Jesus, he threw himself at his feet 23and pleaded with him again and again. “My little daughter is dying,” he said. “Please come and put your hands on her, so that she may get well and live.” 24So Jesus set out with him.

Twelve years of bleeding

A huge crowd went along behind him, jostling him on every side. 25In the crowd was a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years. 26She had gone through a great deal at the hands of many doctors and had spent everything she owned. Instead of getting better, she had only grown worse. 27She had heard about Jesus, so she made her way through the crowd and touched his cloak from behind. 28She kept telling herself, “Even if all I touch is his clothes, I will be made well.” 29At once her bleeding stopped, and she could feel in her body that she was free of her suffering. 30Right away Jesus knew within himself that power had gone out of him. He turned around in the crowd and said, “Who touched my clothes?” 31His disciples said to him, “You can see how the crowd is crushing in on you. How can you ask, ‘Who touched me?’” 32But Jesus went on searching the faces around him for the one who had done it. 33Then the woman, afraid and shaking, knowing what had been done for her, came forward, dropped down before him, and told him the whole truth. 34“Daughter,” he told her, “your faith has saved you and made you well. Go in peace, free of your suffering.”

Little girl, get up

35While Jesus was still talking, some people arrived from the synagogue leader’s house. “Your daughter is dead,” they said. “There is no need to bother the teacher any more.” 36But Jesus paid no attention to what they said and told the synagogue leader, “Do not be afraid. Just believe.” 37He would not let anyone come with him except Peter, James, and James’s brother John. 38When they reached the synagogue leader’s house, Jesus saw an uproar, with people crying and howling in grief. 39He went in and asked them, “Why all this noise and crying? The child is not dead. She is asleep.” 40They laughed at him. But Jesus sent them all outside. Then he took the disciples who were with him and the child’s father and mother, and went into the room where the girl lay. 41He took the child by the hand and said to her, “Talitha koum,” which means, “Little girl, I tell you, get up.” 42At once the girl stood up and walked about, for she was twelve years old. Everyone was astounded on the spot. 43Jesus gave them strict orders not to let anyone find out about this, and said she should be given food.
fields.summary: Across the lake Jesus frees a man possessed by a legion of demons, which go into a herd of pigs. A woman who had bled for twelve years is healed by touching Jesus’s clothes, and the daughter of Jairus is raised from death.

fields.title: Mark 6
fields.body_html:
Rejected in his hometown

1Jesus left that place and went to his hometown, and his disciples went with him. 2When the Sabbath came, he began teaching in the synagogue, and most of those who heard him were struck with amazement. “Where did this man get all this?” they said. “What is this wisdom that has been given to him? And what are these mighty works that his hands are doing?” 3Is he not the carpenter, the son of Mary, and a brother of James, Joses, Judas and Simon? And are his sisters not here among us? And they were offended by him. 4Jesus told them, “Everywhere a prophet is honored, except in his own town, among his own kin, and in his own family.” 5There he was not able to do any mighty work, apart from laying his hands on a few who were sick and healing them. 6Their unbelief amazed him.

The Twelve sent out two by two

Then he went from village to village in that area, teaching. 7He called the Twelve to him and began sending them out in pairs, giving them authority over unclean spirits. 8He told them to take nothing for the journey except a walking stick: no food, no traveler’s bag, and no coins in their belts. 9They were to wear sandals. “And do not put on a second tunic,” he said. 10He told them, “When you go into a house, stay in it until you leave that town. 11Where people will not take you in or hear what you say, shake off the dust from under your feet as you go, as a witness against them.”

12So they went out and called people to repent. 13They threw out demon after demon, and many who were sick they anointed with oil and made well.

Herod hears about Jesus

14King Herod heard about it, for Jesus’ name had become widely known. People were saying, “John the Baptizer has been raised from the dead. That is why these powers are at work in him.” 15Others said, “It is Elijah,” and others again, “He is a prophet, one like the prophets of long ago.” 16But when Herod heard of it, he said, “It is John, the man I beheaded. He has been raised!”

The death of John the Baptizer

17It was Herod himself who had sent men to seize John and had tied him up in prison. He did it on account of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, since he had married her. 18John had kept telling Herod, “The law does not allow you to have your brother’s wife.” 19So Herodias nursed a grudge against John and wanted him dead, but she could not bring it about, 20because Herod stood in awe of John. He knew John was a righteous and holy man, so he kept him safe. Whenever he listened to John, he was left deeply troubled, and yet he liked to hear him.

21At last Herodias had her chance. Herod held a feast on his birthday for the great men of his court, the officers of his army, and the chief men of Galilee. 22Herodias’s own daughter came in and danced, and Herod and those at table with him were delighted with her. So the king told the girl, “Name anything you like, and I will give it to you.” 23He even swore an oath to her: “Anything you ask me for, I will give you, as much as half my kingdom.” 24The girl went out to her mother and said, “What should I ask for?” “The head of John the Baptizer,” her mother answered. 25Straight away she rushed back to the king and made her request. “I want the head of John the Baptist,” she said, “on a platter, and I want it now.” 26This grieved the king deeply. Yet he had sworn oaths in front of his guests, and he was not willing to break his word to her. 27At once the king sent one of his guards with orders to bring John’s head. The man went and beheaded John in the prison. 28He carried the head in on a platter and handed it to the girl, and she handed it to her mother. 29When John’s disciples heard about it, they came for his body and buried it in a tomb.

Five loaves and two fish

30The apostles returned to Jesus and gave him a report of all they had done and all they had taught. 31He said to them, “Come away on your own, to a place without people, and get a little rest.” There was a constant stream of people arriving and leaving, and they could not even find time for a meal. 32So they left in the boat, alone, for a remote spot. 33But many people saw them leaving and knew who they were. People from all the towns hurried there on foot and reached the place before them. 34When Jesus came ashore, he saw a great crowd. He felt deep pity for them, for they were like sheep with no shepherd, and he began to teach them at length.

35By now it was late in the day, and his disciples came to him and said, “No one lives out here, and it is getting late. 36Send the people away, so they can go to the farms and villages round about and get themselves some food.” 37But he replied, “You yourselves give them something to eat.” They said to him, “Are we to go and spend eight months’ wages on bread and give it to them to eat?” 38He asked them, “How many loaves do you have? Go and look.” When they had found out, they told him, “Five, and two fish.” 39Then he ordered them to seat all the people on the green grass in companies, as at a meal. 40So they sat down in groups like the plots of a garden, in hundreds and in fifties. 41Jesus took the five loaves and two fish, looked up to heaven, and spoke a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and handed them again and again to the disciples to serve to the people. And he shared out the two fish among everyone. 42They all ate until they were full. 43Then they gathered up twelve baskets full of broken pieces of bread, and of the fish too. 44The men who had eaten the loaves numbered 5,000.

Across the lake at night

45Right away Jesus pressed his disciples to board the boat and cross ahead of him to Bethsaida on the other side, while he dismissed the crowd. 46After saying goodbye to them, he went off up the mountain to pray.

47When evening came, the boat was far out on the lake, and Jesus was alone on land. 48He saw them struggling at the oars, since the wind was against them. Toward the end of the night, in the fourth watch, he came out to them walking on the lake. He meant to pass by them. 49When they saw him walking on the lake, they took him for a ghost and cried out in fear, 50for every one of them saw him and they were shaken. But right away he spoke to them. “Be brave,” he said. “It is I. Stop being afraid.” 51Then he got into the boat beside them, and the wind dropped. They were beside themselves with amazement, 52for they had not grasped what the loaves showed. Their hearts had been hardened.

Healing at Gennesaret

53When they had crossed the lake, they came ashore at Gennesaret and tied up the boat. 54As soon as they stepped out of the boat, people knew who he was. 55They ran all through that region and began bringing those who were ill on their mats to any place where they heard he was. 56Wherever he went, whether villages or towns or farms, people set their sick down in the marketplaces and pleaded with him to let them touch just the fringe of his cloak. Everyone who touched him was made well.
fields.summary: Jesus is rejected in Nazareth and sends the Twelve out two by two. Herod, who had John the Baptizer beheaded, hears about Jesus; Jesus feeds five thousand with five loaves and two fish, walks on the lake at night and heals the sick at Gennesaret.

fields.title: Mark 7
fields.body_html:
Washed hands and the tradition of the elders

1The Pharisees gathered around Jesus, together with some scribes who had come from Jerusalem. 2They had noticed that some of his disciples were eating their food with unclean hands, that is, hands not washed. 3(The Pharisees, and indeed all the Jews, will not eat unless they give their hands a ritual washing, and so they keep the tradition of the elders. 4When they come in from the marketplace they do not eat without first washing. They hold to many other customs that have been passed on to them as well, such as the washing of cups, pitchers, bronze pots and dining couches.) 5So the Pharisees and the scribes put a question to him: “Why do your disciples not live by the tradition of the elders? Why do they eat with unclean hands?” 6He answered them, “How well Isaiah prophesied about you hypocrites! As it stands written: ‘This people gives me honor with their lips, while their heart stays far away from me. 7Their worship of me is worthless, for they pass off human commands as doctrine.’ 8You abandon what God has commanded and hold fast to a tradition that is merely human.”

9He went on, “You are very skillful at setting God’s command aside so that you can keep your own tradition! 10For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and also, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother is to die for it.’ 11But you teach that if someone tells father or mother, ‘Whatever support you could have had from me is Corban’ (which means an offering to God), 12then you no longer let that person do anything for their father or mother. 13You make God’s word empty for the sake of the tradition you hand down, and you do plenty of other things of the same kind.”

What makes a person unclean

14Then he called the crowd to him once more and said, “Hear me, every one of you, and understand this: 15Nothing outside a person can make that person unclean by going in. What comes out of a person is what makes a person unclean.”

17When he had left the crowd and gone indoors, his disciples asked him about this parable. 18He said to them, “Are even you so slow to understand? Do you not see that nothing that goes into a person from outside can make that person unclean? 19It does not go into the heart but into the stomach, and from there it goes out into the latrine.” By saying this, Jesus made all foods clean. 20He went on, “What comes out of a person is what makes a person unclean. 21Out of the human heart, from within, come evil designs, sexual sin, theft, murder, 22adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, indecency, envy, slander, pride, and moral folly. 23All these evils come out from inside, and they are what make a person unclean.”

Even the little dogs eat the crumbs

24Jesus set out from there and went away to the region around Tyre. He went into a house and did not want anyone to know, but he could not stay hidden. 25A woman whose young daughter had an unclean spirit heard about him at once, and she came and threw herself down at his feet. 26The woman was a Gentile, born in Syrian Phoenicia. She kept begging him to throw the demon out of her daughter. 27He told her, “The children must be fed first and have all they want. Taking the children’s bread and throwing it to the little dogs is not right.” 28She replied, “Lord, even the little dogs under the table get to eat the crumbs the children drop.” 29He told her, “Because of what you have said, go on your way. The demon has already gone out of your daughter.” 30When she got home, she found her little girl stretched out on the bed, and the demon had gone.

Ephphatha: be opened

31Then he left the region of Tyre again and went by way of Sidon to the lake of Galilee, into the Decapolis region. 32They brought him a deaf man who could hardly speak, and they pleaded with him to place his hand on him. 33Jesus led him off from the crowd to be alone with him. He pushed his fingers into the man’s ears, spat, and touched his tongue. 34Then he looked up to heaven, groaned, and said to him, “Ephphatha,” meaning, “Be opened.” 35His ears were opened, his tongue was set free from what bound it, and he spoke clearly. 36Jesus told them to say nothing to anyone. Yet the more he gave this order, the more eagerly they spread the news. 37The people were utterly astounded. “How well he has done everything!” they said. “He gives hearing to the deaf and speech to those who cannot talk!”
fields.summary: Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for setting aside God’s command for human tradition and teaches that what makes a person unclean comes from within. A Gentile woman from Syrian Phoenicia wins healing for her daughter, and a deaf man is healed with the word “Ephphatha”, “Be opened.”

fields.title: Mark 8
fields.body_html:
Seven loaves in a deserted place

1During those days a large crowd had gathered again, and there was no food for them. So Jesus called his disciples to him and said to them, 2“My heart goes out to these people. They have been with me for three days now, and they have nothing left to eat. 3Send them home without food, and they will collapse on the road. Some of them have traveled a long way.” 4His disciples replied, “Out here in this empty country, where could anyone find bread enough to fill all these people?” 5He asked them, “How many loaves have you got?” “Seven,” they answered. 6He had the crowd sit on the ground. Taking the seven loaves, he gave thanks, broke them, and kept handing them to his disciples to pass around, and they served them to the crowd. 7They also had a few small fish. He blessed them and told the disciples to hand those out too. 8Everyone ate and had plenty. Then they collected the leftover pieces, enough to fill seven large baskets. 9There were about 4,000 people. Then he sent them on their way. 10At once he boarded the boat with his disciples and came to the area of Dalmanutha.

No sign for this generation

11The Pharisees came out and started to dispute with him. They demanded a sign from heaven, to put him to the test. 12He groaned from deep within and said, “Why does this generation look for a sign? Truly I tell you, this generation will be given no sign at all.” 13Leaving them, he got into the boat again and went off to the far shore.

Do you still not understand?

14Now the disciples had forgotten to bring bread. They had just one loaf with them in the boat. 15He gave them a warning: “Be careful! Watch out for the Pharisees’ yeast and Herod’s yeast.” 16They began to talk it over among themselves: they had no bread. 17Jesus knew what they were saying, and he said, “Why are you talking about having no bread? Do you still not see it or understand? Have your hearts been hardened? 18You have eyes; can you not see? You have ears; can you not hear? Do you not remember? 19When I broke five loaves for the 5,000, how many baskets of leftover pieces did you gather?” “Twelve,” they told him. 20“And when I broke seven loaves for the 4,000, how many large baskets of pieces did you gather?” “Seven,” they said. 21He said to them, “And you still do not understand?” 22They came to Bethsaida. Some people brought a blind man to him and pleaded with him to touch him. 23He took hold of the blind man’s hand and took him outside the village. Then he spat on the man’s eyes, laid his hands on him, and asked, “Can you see anything?” 24The man looked up and said, “I see people, but to me they are like trees moving about.” 25Then Jesus laid his hands on the man’s eyes once more. The man looked hard, his sight came back, and he could see everything clearly. 26Jesus sent him off home, telling him, “Do not even set foot in the village.”

You are Christ

27Jesus and his disciples set out for the villages of the Caesarea Philippi area. As they went, he asked them, “Who do people say I am?” 28They answered, “Some say John the Baptist; some, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.” 29“And you,” he asked them, “who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ.” 30He gave them strict orders not to tell anyone about him.

The Son of Man must suffer

31He then began teaching them that the Son of Man had to undergo great suffering, be rejected by elders, chief priests and scribes, be put to death, and rise again after three days. 32He spoke about this quite plainly. Peter took him to one side and began to rebuke him. 33But Jesus turned and looked at his disciples, and he rebuked Peter. “Get behind me, Satan!” he said. “Your mind is not on what God cares about, but on what people care about.”

Take up your cross

34Then he called the crowd over, together with his disciples, and said to them, “If anyone desires to come after me, they must say no to themselves, take up their cross, and follow me. 35Anyone set on keeping their life safe will lose it, and anyone who loses their life because of me and the gospel will save it. 36What does anyone gain by winning the whole world, if it costs them their life? 37What could anyone give to buy their life back? 38Whoever is ashamed of me and of what I say, here among this adulterous, sinful generation, the Son of Man will in turn be ashamed of them, when he comes with the holy angels in the glory of his Father.”
fields.summary: Jesus feeds four thousand with seven loaves, refuses the Pharisees a sign, warns about their yeast and heals a blind man at Bethsaida. At Caesarea Philippi Peter declares who Jesus is, and Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, die and rise, and that followers must take up their cross.

fields.title: Mark 9
fields.body_html:
1He went on to say to them, “Truly I tell you, some who stand here will not taste death until the kingdom of God has come in power and they have seen it.”

Transfigured on the mountain

2Six days later Jesus took Peter, James and John with him and led them up a high mountain, away from everyone else. There he was transfigured in front of them. 3His clothes turned dazzling and intensely white, white beyond what any launderer on earth could achieve. 4Then Elijah appeared to them along with Moses, and the two were talking with Jesus. 5Peter spoke up and said to Jesus, “Rabbi, how good it is that we are here! Let us set up three shelters, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” 6He did not know what to say, because they were all badly frightened. 7Then a cloud came and cast its shadow over them, and a voice spoke from the cloud: “This is my dearly loved Son. Listen to him.” 8All at once they looked around and saw no one there with them any more, only Jesus.

Elijah has come

9As they came down the mountain, he gave them orders not to describe what they had seen to anyone until the Son of Man rose from the dead. 10They kept the matter to themselves, but they debated with one another what this “rising from the dead” might mean. 11They asked him, “Why do the scribes claim that Elijah has to come first?” 12He told them, “Elijah does come first and set everything right. Then why does Scripture say that the Son of Man is to suffer much and be scorned? 13But I tell you that Elijah has in fact come, and they did to him as they pleased, just as it is written about him.”

I believe; help my unbelief

14When they got back to the other disciples, they found a large crowd surrounding them, and some scribes disputing with them. 15As soon as the people saw him, the whole crowd was overcome with wonder, and they ran up to greet him. 16He asked them, “What are you arguing with them about?” 17A man in the crowd answered him, “Teacher, I brought my son to you. He has a spirit that makes him unable to speak. 18Whenever it takes hold of him, it dashes him to the ground, and he foams at the mouth, grinds his teeth, and goes stiff. I asked your disciples to throw it out, but they did not have the strength.” 19Jesus answered them, “You unbelieving generation! How long must I stay with you? How long must I bear with you? Bring the boy to me.” 20So they brought the boy to him. As soon as the spirit saw Jesus, it threw the boy into a fit. He fell to the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. 21Jesus asked the boy’s father, “Since when has this been happening to him?” He answered, “Since he was a small child. 22Many times it has thrown him into fire or into water to kill him. But if you are able to do anything at all, help us. Have pity on us!” 23Jesus said to him, “‘If you can!’ All things are possible for the one who believes.” 24At once the boy’s father cried out, “I believe! Help my unbelief!” 25When Jesus saw that a crowd was quickly gathering, he gave the unclean spirit a stern order: “You mute and deaf spirit, I command you to come out of him and never go into him again!” 26The spirit shrieked, threw him into violent convulsions, and came out. The boy was left lying like a corpse, so that most of them said, “He has died.” 27But Jesus took hold of his hand and lifted him up, and he got to his feet. 28After he went indoors, his disciples asked him privately, “Why could we not throw it out?” 29He told them, “This kind cannot be made to come out by any means except prayer.”

Handed over, killed, and raised

30They left that place and made their way through Galilee. Jesus did not want anyone to know where they were, 31for he was busy teaching his disciples. “The Son of Man is going to be handed over into human hands,” he told them. “They will kill him, and three days after he is killed he will rise again.” 32But they did not grasp what he meant, and they were afraid to question him.

Who is the greatest?

33They arrived at Capernaum. Once they were inside the house, he asked them, “What was it you were debating as we walked?” 34They said nothing, because on the way they had been debating among themselves which of them was the greatest. 35He sat down, called the Twelve, and said to them, “Whoever wants to be first must be last of everyone and the servant of everyone.” 36He took a little child and stood the child among them. Then, putting his arms around the child, he said to them, 37“Whoever welcomes a child like this one in my name is welcoming me. And whoever welcomes me is welcoming, not me, but the One who sent me.”

Whoever is not against us

38John said to him, “Teacher, we saw a man throwing out demons in your name. We tried to stop him, since he did not go around with us.” 39Jesus said, “Do not stop him. No one who does a mighty work in my name will be quick to speak ill of me afterward. 40Anyone not against us is for us.

41If anyone gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ, truly I tell you, that person will certainly not lose the reward.

Better to enter life maimed

42Whoever makes one of these little ones who believe in me fall away would be better off having a huge millstone hung around the neck and being thrown into the sea.

43If your hand leads you into sin, cut it off. You are better off entering life maimed than going off with both hands into hell, into the fire that cannot be put out. 45If your foot leads you into sin, cut it off. You are better off entering life lame than being thrown into hell with both feet. 47If your eye leads you into sin, tear it out. You are better off entering the kingdom of God with only one eye than being thrown into hell with two, 48where the worm that eats them never dies and the fire is never put out.

49Everyone will be salted with fire. 50Salt is a good thing. But if the salt stops being salty, how will you give it back its flavor? Have salt in yourselves, and live in peace with one another.”
fields.summary: Jesus is transfigured on a mountain before Peter, James and John, and afterward frees a boy from an unclean spirit when his father cries, “I believe; help my unbelief.” Jesus again foretells death and rising, and teaches that whoever wants to be first must be servant of all.

fields.title: Mark 10
fields.body_html:
What God has joined

1Jesus set out from there and came to the districts of Judea and the land beyond the Jordan. Crowds came together around him again, and he taught them once more, as he usually did.

2Some people asked him whether the law allows a husband to divorce his wife. They were trying to trap him. 3He replied with a question: “What did Moses command you?” 4They said, “Moses allowed a man to write out a certificate of divorce and send his wife away.” 5But Jesus told them, “It was because your hearts were hard that Moses wrote this commandment for you. 6But at the beginning, when the world was created, God made them male and female. 7‘This is why a man will leave his father and his mother and be joined to his wife, 8and the two of them will be one flesh.’ And so they are two no longer, but one flesh. 9What God has yoked together, then, no human being is to separate.”

10Back in the house, the disciples asked him about this again. 11He told them, “A man commits adultery against his wife if he divorces her and marries another woman. 12And a woman who divorces her husband and marries another man commits adultery.”

Let the children come

13People were bringing young children to him so that he would touch them, but the disciples scolded them. 14When Jesus saw this, he was angry and told them, “Allow the children to come to me. Do not try to stop them, because it is to people like them that the kingdom of God belongs. 15Truly I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God the way a child does will never get into it.” 16Then he took the children in his arms, laid his hands on them, and blessed them.

A rich man’s question

17As Jesus was setting out on his journey, a man ran up to him, fell on his knees in front of him, and asked, “Good Teacher, what should I do to inherit eternal life?” 18Jesus answered, “Why are you calling me good? No one is good except God alone. 19You know what the commandments say: ‘Do not murder. Do not commit adultery. Do not steal. Do not testify falsely. Do not cheat anyone. Honor your father and mother.’” 20“Teacher,” he replied, “I have obeyed all of these since I was a boy.” 21Jesus looked at him and loved him. “You are missing one thing,” he told him. “Go and sell everything you own, and give the money to the poor. Then you will have treasure in heaven. After that, come and follow me.” 22At these words his face clouded over, and he went away sad, for he owned a great deal of property.

23Jesus looked around and told his disciples, “How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!” 24The disciples were amazed at what he said. But Jesus said to them again, “My children, how hard it is to get into the kingdom of God! 25A camel could pass through the eye of a needle more easily than a rich person could enter the kingdom of God.” 26They were utterly amazed and said to each other, “Who can be saved, then?” 27Jesus looked straight at them and said, “For human beings it cannot be done, but not for God. God can do anything.”

28Peter spoke up: “Look, we have left everything behind to follow you.” 29Jesus said, “Truly I tell you, anyone who has left a home, brothers or sisters, mother or father, children or land because of me and because of the gospel 30will receive a hundred times as much now, in this present time: homes, brothers, sisters, mothers, children and land, together with persecutions. And in the age that is coming they will receive eternal life. 31Yet many who are first will end up last, and the last first.”

On the road up to Jerusalem

32They were on the road going up to Jerusalem, with Jesus going on ahead of them. The disciples were astonished, and the others who followed were afraid. Again he took the Twelve with him and began telling them the things that were about to happen to him. 33“We are on our way up to Jerusalem,” he said, “and there the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, who will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles. 34They will make fun of him, spit on him, whip him and kill him; and three days later he will rise.”

Not to be served but to serve

35Then James and John, Zebedee’s sons, came up to him. “Teacher,” they said, “we would like you to do whatever we ask of you.” 36“What would you like me to do for you?” he asked them. 37They answered, “Grant that when you are in your glory, one of us may sit on your right and one on your left.” 38Jesus said to them, “You have no idea what you are asking for. Can you drink the cup that I am drinking, or be baptized with the baptism I am going through?” 39“We can,” they told him. Jesus told them, “The cup I drink, you will drink, and with the baptism I am going through you too will be baptized. 40But a seat at my right or at my left is not mine to grant. Those places belong to the ones for whom they have been prepared.”

41When the other ten heard about this, they became angry with James and John. 42Jesus called them to him and told them, “You know that those who are thought of as rulers of the nations lord it over their people, and their important men use their power over them. 43That is not how it is among you. Instead, whoever among you wants to become great must be your servant, 44and whoever among you wants to be first must serve everyone as a slave. 45The Son of Man himself came, not so that others would serve him, but to serve them and to give his life as the ransom price for many.”

Blind Bartimaeus

46Then they came to Jericho. As he was going out of Jericho with his disciples and a large crowd, Bartimaeus son of Timaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting beside the road. 47When he heard it was Jesus of Nazareth, he started to shout, “Son of David, Jesus, have mercy on me!” 48Many people scolded him and told him to keep quiet, but he kept shouting even more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” 49Jesus stood still and said, “Call him over.” So they called to the blind man and told him, “Take courage! Get up! He is calling you.” 50He threw off his cloak, sprang to his feet and came to Jesus. 51Jesus said to him in reply, “What would you like me to do for you?” The blind man said to him, “Rabbouni, I want to see again.” 52Jesus told him, “Go. Your faith has saved you and made you well.” At once his sight came back, and he followed him along the road.
fields.summary: Jesus teaches that what God has joined no one should separate, welcomes the children and tells a rich man to sell everything and follow. On the road to Jerusalem Jesus foretells death a third time, says the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and gives sight to blind Bartimaeus.

fields.title: Mark 11
fields.body_html:
Hosanna on the road to Jerusalem

1As they were approaching Jerusalem and came near Bethphage and Bethany, by the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent off two of his disciples 2with these instructions: “Go to the village ahead of you. The moment you go in, you will find a colt tied up there that no one has ever ridden. Untie it and bring it here. 3Should anyone ask you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ tell them, ‘The Lord needs it, and he will send it back here without delay.’” 4They went off and found a colt tied by a doorway, out in the street, and they untied it. 5Some of the people standing nearby asked them, “What do you mean by untying that colt?” 6The disciples answered as Jesus had told them, and the people let them go. 7They brought the colt to Jesus and laid their cloaks over its back, and he sat on it. 8Many people spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches they had cut in the fields. 9The people walking in front and those coming behind kept shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord’s name! 10Blessed be the kingdom of our father David, now coming! Hosanna in highest heaven!”

11Jesus went into Jerusalem and into the temple courts. He looked all around at everything, but because it was already late in the day, he left for Bethany with the Twelve.

A fig tree with nothing but leaves

12The next day, as they were leaving Bethany, Jesus was hungry. 13Seeing at a distance a fig tree covered in leaves, he went over to find out whether there was anything on it. When he reached it, he found nothing but leaves, because it was not the time of year for figs. 14He told the tree, “Let no one eat fruit from you ever again.” And his disciples heard it.

A house of prayer for all the nations

15Then they came into Jerusalem. He went into the temple courts and began driving out the people who were selling and buying there. He turned over the money changers’ tables and the benches of the dove sellers, 16and he would not let anyone carry goods through the temple courts. 17Then he taught them, saying, “Does Scripture not say, ‘My house will be known as a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have turned it into a hideout for bandits.” 18When the chief priests and the scribes heard about this, they began looking for a way to do away with him. They feared him, since the whole crowd was spellbound by his teaching.

19And each evening they went out of the city.

Have faith in God

20Early the next day, as they went along, they saw the fig tree withered from the roots up. 21Peter remembered and said to him, “Look, Rabbi! The fig tree you cursed is all dried up.” 22Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God. 23Truly I tell you, if anyone tells this mountain, ‘Rise up and be hurled into the sea,’ and does not waver in their heart, but believes that what they say is taking place, it will be done for them. 24So I tell you: everything you request when you pray, believe that you received it, and you will have it. 25And whenever you stand up to pray, if you are holding anything against anyone, forgive them, so that your Father in heaven may forgive you your wrongdoings as well.”

By what authority?

27They came back into Jerusalem once more. As he was walking in the temple courts, the chief priests, the scribes and the elders came up to him 28and demanded, “What authority do you have for doing these things? Or who is it that gave you this authority to do them?” 29Jesus said to them, “I will put one question to you. Answer me, and then I will tell you what authority I have for doing these things. 30John’s baptism: did it come from heaven, or from human beings? Answer me!” 31They talked it over among themselves: “What are we to say? If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will reply, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’ 32But suppose we say, ‘From human beings’ . . .” They were afraid of the crowd, because everyone held that John was truly a prophet. 33So they replied to Jesus, “We do not know.” Jesus said to them, “Then I am not telling you what authority I have for doing these things, either.”
fields.summary: Jesus enters Jerusalem to shouts of “Hosanna”, curses a fig tree that has nothing but leaves and drives the traders out of the temple, a house of prayer for all the nations. Jesus urges faith in God and answers the leaders’ question about authority with a question about John’s baptism.

fields.title: Mark 12
fields.body_html:
The tenants of the vineyard

1Then he began to teach them in parables. “There was a man who planted a vineyard and put a hedge around it. He dug a vat below the winepress and built a lookout tower. Then he leased the vineyard to tenant farmers and went to another country. 2When harvest time came, he sent a servant to the tenants to collect from them his share of the vineyard’s crop. 3But they seized him, beat him and sent him off with nothing. 4He sent them another servant, and they struck this one on the head and insulted him. 5He sent yet another, and him they killed. It went the same way with many others: some they beat, and some they killed. 6He had one left to send, his dearly loved son. Last of all he sent him to them, thinking, ‘They will show respect for my son.’ 7But the tenants talked it over among themselves: ‘This is the heir. Come on, we will put him to death, and the vineyard will be ours to keep.’ 8So they seized him, put him to death and threw his body out of the vineyard. 9So what will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and put those tenants to death, and he will hand the vineyard over to others. 10Have you not even read this passage of Scripture: ‘The stone that the builders threw away as useless has become the chief cornerstone. 11This was the Lord’s doing, and we look on it with wonder’?” 12The leaders wanted to arrest him, but they were afraid of the crowd. They knew that he had aimed the parable at them. So they left him and went off.

Give back to Caesar

13Then they sent some Pharisees and Herodians to him, to trap him with his own words. 14They came and said to him, “Teacher, we are sure that you are a man of integrity and that you are not swayed by anyone. You pay no attention to a person’s rank, but you teach the way of God in truth. Is it right to pay the tax to Caesar, or not? Are we to pay or not?” 15But he saw through their pretense and said to them, “Why are you trying to trap me? Bring me a silver coin worth a day’s wage so I can look at it.” 16They brought one. He asked them, “Whose face is this, and whose name is written here?” “Caesar’s,” they told him. 17Jesus said to them, “Pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God.” They were astonished at him.

The God of the living

18Then some Sadducees came to him. They say there is no resurrection, and they put a question to him: 19“Teacher, Moses gave us this rule in writing: if a man dies and leaves a wife but no child, his brother is to marry the widow and father children to carry on the dead man’s family. 20Once there were seven brothers. The first of them married, and he died without leaving any children. 21The second brother married her and died, again leaving no children, and the third did the same. 22None of the seven left any children. Last of all, the woman died too. 23At the resurrection, when they rise again, which of them will she be married to? All seven had her as their wife.” 24Jesus said to them, “Is not this the reason you are mistaken: you know neither the Scriptures nor God’s power? 25When people rise from the dead, there is no marrying or being given in marriage. They are like the angels in heaven. 26As for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God said to him, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? 27He is not the God of the dead but of the living. How badly you have gone astray!”

The first commandment of all
